title: Self-Induced Outcome Potential: Turn-Level Credit Assignment for Agents without Verifiers

paper.title: Self-Induced Outcome Potential: Turn-Level Credit Assignment for Agents without Verifiers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-horizon LLM agents succeed or fail through intermediate information-gathering turns, yet training signals are usually observed only at the final answer, because process-level rewards require extensive high-quality human annotation. Existing turn-level shaping methods address this supervision mismatch by rewarding turns that increase the likelihood of a gold answer, but they require answer supervision or stable task-specific verifiers that are often unavailable in agentic settings. Conversely, recent label-free reinforcement learning (RL) methods extract useful self-signals from output distributions, but mostly at the answer or trajectory level and therefore cannot attribute value to intermediate turns. To address these issues, we propose Self-Induced Outcome Potential (SIOP), a framework that treats semantic clusters of final answers as latent future outcome states for potential-based turn-level credit assignment. For each query, we sample multiple rollouts, cluster their final answers into semantic outcome modes, and construct a reliability-aware target distribution over these latent states. We first formulate a distributional potential that rewards turns for increasing posterior support for reliable future outcome states, and then instantiate it with a tractable cluster-level approximation. Terminal outcome mass is added only at the final answer turn and propagated backward through turn-level advantages. The resulting objective generalizes information-potential shaping from gold-answer supervision to settings without task-specific gold verifiers while avoiding the broadcasted rollout-level advantages used by standard GRPO.
We formalize the framework, establish its reduction to supervised turn-level shaping in the gold-answer limit, and show that SIOP consistently improves over verifier-free outcome-level baselines on seven search-augmented agentic reasoning benchmarks while approaching the average performance of a gold-supervised outcome baseline.
Code is available at https://github.com/dl-m9/SIOP.git .

Code is available at https://github.com/dl-m9/SIOP.git . 1 Introduction Recent reasoning models such as OpenAI o1 [ 1 ] and DeepSeek-R1 [ 2 ] have made a broader shift visible: large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to solve problems through extended reasoning rather than immediate answer generation. Agentic settings extend this paradigm from internal reasoning traces to external interaction. Instead of answering from a fixed prompt, an agent reasons over a partial state, retrieves evidence, calls tools, observes returned information, and decides whether further interaction is needed. This turns model behavior from static generation into sequential decision making over reasoning, tool use, and external observations. The shift is visible across recent systems and training recipes. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems surveyed by Li et al. [ 3 ] frame retrieval as adaptive interaction rather than static preprocessing. Kimi K2 [ 4 ] uses large-scale agentic data synthesis and joint reinforcement learning through real and synthetic environments. ReSearch [ 5 ] and Search-R1 [ 6 ] train search-augmented models to interleave reasoning and retrieval. ToolRL [ 7 ] and SimpleTIR [ 8 ] study tool-use RL and tool-integrated reasoning under multi-turn interaction. These works show that agentic RL has become a practical path for improving interactive reasoning. However, many of these training recipes still rely on outcome-level feedback: the policy receives rewards mainly from final-answer correctness, task success, or terminal score after the full trajectory is complete. Such outcome-only reinforcement learning is not well suited to interactive agents. In long trajectories, a single terminal reward cannot reliably identify whether a specific thought, tool call, or observation improved the agent’s future prospects. For example, ReasonRAG [ 9 ] and InForage [ 10 ] report that outcome-supervised agentic RL suffers from low exploration efficiency, gradient conflict, and sparse rewards. These studies indicate that terminal outcome supervision is not enough to guide the agent’s long-horizon behavior. To address this problem, one line of work proposes turn-level reward shaping. For example, methods such as IGPO [ 11 ] , Δ \Delta Belief-RL [ 12 ] , TIPS [ 13 ] , and InfoPO [ 14 ] measure whether an interaction turn increases the model’s support for a desired target, such as the gold answer or the correct next action. These methods show that information-potential shaping can substantially improve multi-turn optimization. However, these methods inherit a strong assumption: a rewardable target must already be available. In many agentic tasks, there is no unique gold answer or stable task-specific verifier against which a turn-level potential can be computed. Another line of work removes this requirement by extracting training signals directly from model outputs. EMPO [ 15 ] clusters semantically equivalent responses and optimizes semantic entropy without external supervision, while TTRL [ 16 ] performs test-time reinforcement learning by selecting the majority answer from repeated samples as a self-generated pseudo-target. Related verifier-free RL methods, including RLPR [ 17 ] , NOVER [ 18 ] , and DRO [ 19 ] , similarly show that model-internal confidence or answer distributions can support learning beyond tasks with explicit verifiers. Yet these methods remain mostly outcome-level: they tell the model which final responses appear more reliable, but not which intermediate turns actually moved the trajectory toward those outcomes. Building on these gaps, this paper studies how to lift unlabeled outcome-level reliability signals into turn-level credit assignment. Our key abstraction is to cluster sampled final answers into semantic outcome modes , where each mode is a query-specific group of answers that express the same underlying meaning, and then treat these modes as latent future states . Even without gold answers or stable task-specific verifiers, a batch of rollouts for the same query induces a structured distribution over these latent states. Some modes are frequent, consistent, evidence-supported, or otherwise more trustworthy than others, while others reflect low-consensus noise and should be down-weighted. We then define a potential function over this self-induced latent state space and reward each turn by how much it increases the model’s support for reliable future outcome states. The resulting self-induced outcome potential generalizes information-potential shaping from gold-answer supervision to verifier-free settings without task-specific gold verifiers. Concretely, we sample multiple full rollouts for each query, cluster their final answers into semantic outcome modes, and assign soft reliability weights to these modes. This yields a distributional target over reliable latent futures rather than a hard pseudo-label. Because estimating the full mode distribution at every turn is expensive, we instantiate this principle in practice with a multi-reference cluster-level approximation that conditions each rollout on its realized semantic outcome mode while scoring a small set of reference answers rather than a single prototype. Terminal outcome mass is added only at the final answer turn and propagated backward through turn-level advantages, so different turns of the same rollout receive different credit. This design preserves the key intuition behind potential-based shaping, namely rewarding the intermediate interactions that move the trajectory toward reliable future states, while avoiding the assumption that a gold answer is known during training. Our contributions are summarized as follows. 1. We formulate verifier-free turn-level credit assignment as potential-based learning over self-induced semantic outcome modes, where clustered final answers serve as latent future states rather than fixed gold targets or trajectory-level pseudo-labels. 2. We define a self-induced outcome potential (SIOP) over these latent states, calibrating empirical outcome modes by reliability signals and converting prefix-to-prefix changes in cluster support into turn-level process rewards. 3. We construct turn-specific advantages for long-horizon agents, assigning credit only to trainable tokens within each turn rather than broadcasting a trajectory-level score. 4. We provide theoretical characterizations showing how the proposed reward reduces to gold-answer shaping in the supervised limit and why it measures step-wise marginal support gain rather than broadcasting a trajectory score. We also present an empirical study on seven search-QA benchmarks showing that our method outperforms outcome-only verifier-free baselines and approaches a gold-supervised outcome RL baseline. 2 Problem Setup We study an agentic setting where an agent receives a query q q and interacts with an environment over multiple turns before producing a final answer. At turn t t , the agent emits reasoning tokens, optionally issues a tool call, and receives an observation. (4) Supervision mismatch. Supervised turn-level shaping methods such as Δ \Delta Belief-RL [ 12 ] , IGPO [ 11 ] , and TIPS [ 13 ] assume access to a gold answer y ⋆ y^{\star} or an equivalent target representation. In our setting, training does not observe a unique correct answer, a stable answer set, or a task-specific correctness verifier. The task-specific information available during learning consists of sampled rollouts from the current policy. Verifier-free terminology. We use verifier-free in the task-specific sense: training requires no gold answers, task-specific correctness verifiers, or hand-designed rewards.
